title: We asked Fable 5 for a game. Then we asked for 227 more.
author: gameover_com
selftext:
Not once, cherry-picked, but again and again, across genres that have almost nothing in common. Each game is a single HTML file that loads in the browser. They're not complete games at this time but a way to poke at the boundaries of Fable 5 for game creation. We're figuring out where things break and iterating on some games. We're also benchmarking Sol and Grok 4.5. The failure cases are just as interesting as the successes.   
  
Sharing playable prototypes and research results at [gameover.com/labs](https://gameover.com/labs/) because they were a genuinely fun thing to build.

comments.author: pxp121kr
comments.body: I'd add tracking, to see how much time players spend on each game, it's useful, maybe also top views etc

replies.author: gameover_com
replies.body: Great idea, thank you. Time spent game is the clearest signal for playability.  We'll look at adding something lightweight for the next round.

comments.author: Quind1
comments.body: Very interesting concept. Like the other poster said, it would be nice to see some usage metrics. I'll be checking these out.

replies.author: gameover_com
replies.body: Thank you for the feedback! Metrics is definitely a solid ask. We'll see what we can put together for the next round.

comments.author: DaedalusRaistlin
comments.body:
Well dang, I thought it was doing well with my 9 playable game concepts and another 8 designed. 

I'm struggling to think of fun game ideas. A lot of these recent ones are just exploring where I can take some recent tech I made with WebGPU, tens of thousands of units on screen and swarm mechanics. But the ideas well is running dry.

replies.author: gameover_com
replies.body: Hi! Nine playable and eight designed is already lot more than most people will get to making. Swarms are a fun constraint. Are you the swarm, fighting it, herding it, feeding it, outrunning it, splitting it? Is the swarm a resource, a terrain, or something that moves and shifts? Are there multiple swarms and you choose the location and conditions where they collide? Feels like there's some room to experiment on.

replies.author: DaedalusRaistlin
replies.body:
Thanks! 

All of those in different games lol. The first one, you control the swarm - give it attack targets, avoid markers, or just let it try to find its own way. When you place two attack markers it's fun to watch the swarm divide. The swarm is a resource, with an upgradeable reinforcement rate and stats like damage and health. It's got destructable walls and structures, and a definitive objective (destroy the tower) before you move onto the next level. 

Another game I'm trying uses the units as visible supply lines in an RTS game. Destroying supply lines is easy once they're found, and the idea is to break the enemies supply chains long enough to starve their production chains. The swarm moves yoiur resources, like a living conveyer belt system. And of course, huge battles involving tens of thousands of vehicles ans infantry. This one is going to have even more destruction - craters blown in the terrain, buildings collapsing and blocking streets, etc. And multiplayer. 

Another one you're just one soldier in a sea of thousands, engaging in melee combat. When you die you posses another soldier. Lots of individual companies moving in formation. 

Another one is trying to recreate the Whiskey Outpost scene from Starship Troopers (first movie) - a single outpost vs thousands of incoming aliens. 

I want to show off a level of scale I've really only seen in 2D games and Ultimate Epic Battle Simulator. But in 3D in the browser. 

In the first game I just got 50k attackers vs 50k defenders working at around 60fps. Hoping to push the numbers higher, defenders were slowing things down at high numbers.

replies.author: gameover_com
replies.body: Sounds interesting. Keep us posted on how the games turn out. Should be fun to play test the games when they are demo-ready.

comments.author: nexe
comments.body: Hm at first this looked like a really cool idea. Now that I've play tested a dozen or so I must unfortunately say that one shotting isn't the way to a good game ;) You gotta put more effort into polishing and testing otherwise its really not a good look

replies.author: gameover_com
replies.body: Really appreciate the useful feedback. Even the most capable models today can't get there in one pass. Part of what we wanted was to see exactly where that limit sits, across a lot of genres, warts and all. We're working on the next experiment for a subset: 15 passes per game, open-ended, directed, or with human feedback. Curious to explore how much of the gap that closes.

replies.author: nexe
replies.body: Yea i think that makes more sense. Good luck 🤞

comments.author: SurvivalHermit
comments.body: See this is what AI is great for protype 200 games in almost no time. get some hands on time with concepts that maybe have never been tried. quickly test interactions between different mechanics. so dope.

replies.author: gameover_com
replies.body: Well said! AI lowers the time and cost of experimentation, but it's up to the designer to make the game actually fun.
